## Introduction

```{r}
rm(list = ls())
library(tidyverse)
library(zoo)
library(tseries)
library(forecast)
library(dynlm)
library(vars)

tryCatch({
  unemployment_data <- read_csv("unemployment_data_gbr.csv")
  gdp_data <- read_csv("gdp_data_gbr.csv")
}, error = function(err) {
  
  library(rsdmx)
  
  oecd_url <- "https://sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/OECD.SDD.TPS,DSD_LFS@DF_IALFS_UNE_M,1.0/AUS+AUT+BEL+CAN+CHL+COL+CRI+CZE+DNK+EST+FIN+FRA+DEU+GRC+HUN+ISL+IRL+ISR+ITA+JPN+KOR+LVA+LTU+LUX+MEX+NLD+NZL+NOR+POL+PRT+SVK+SVN+ESP+SWE+CHE+TUR+GBR+USA+G7+EA20+EU27_2020+OECD+BGR+HRV+ROU..._Z.Y._T.Y_GE15..Q?startPeriod=1980-Q1&endPeriod=2025-Q4&dimensionAtObservation=AllDimensions" 
  oecd_url2 <- "https://sdmx.oecd.org/public/rest/data/OECD.SDD.NAD,DSD_NAMAIN1@DF_QNA_EXPENDITURE_GROWTH_OECD,1.1/Q..GBR...B1GQ......G1.?startPeriod=1985-Q1&dimensionAtObservation=AllDimensions"
  sdmx_obj <- readSDMX(oecd_url)
  sdmx_obj2 <- readSDMX(oecd_url2)
  
  unemployment_data <- as.data.frame(sdmx_obj)
  gdp_data <- as.data.frame(sdmx_obj2)
# save to csv
write_csv(unemployment_data, "unemployment_data_gbr.csv")  
write_csv(gdp_data, "gdp_data_gbr.csv")
}
)

unemployment_data <-read_csv("unemployment_data_gbr.csv") %>%
  filter(REF_AREA == "GBR", TIME_PERIOD >= '1985-Q1') %>%
  rename(unemployment_rate = obsValue) %>%
mutate(year = as.numeric(substr(TIME_PERIOD, 1, 4)),
    quarter = as.numeric(substr(TIME_PERIOD, 7, 7))
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(year, quarter, REF_AREA, unemployment_rate)


unemployment_ts <- ts(
  unemployment_data$unemployment_rate,
  start = c(min(unemployment_data$year), min(unemployment_data$quarter)),
  frequency = 4
)

gdp_data <-read_csv("gdp_data_gbr.csv") %>%
  rename(gdp_rate = obsValue) %>%
mutate(year = as.numeric(substr(TIME_PERIOD, 1, 4)),
    quarter = as.numeric(substr(TIME_PERIOD, 7, 7))
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(year, quarter, REF_AREA,gdp_rate)

gdp_ts <- ts(
  gdp_data$gdp_rate,
  start = c(min(gdp_data$year), min(gdp_data$quarter)),
  frequency = 4
)

# combine the two datasets
df <- left_join(unemployment_data, gdp_data, by = c("year", "quarter", "REF_AREA")) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(unemployment_rate, gdp_rate),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(variable = recode(variable,
    unemployment_rate = "Unemployment Rate (%)",
    gdp_rate = "GDP Growth (%)"
  ))


df$date <- as.Date(as.yearqtr(paste(df$year, df$quarter), "%Y %q"))
```

- United Kingdom

- Unemployment rate and economic growth

- Time Series Analysis
  - ARIMA / ARMIAX
  - Cointegration
  - VAR

:::{.notes}

- We study how unemployment and economic growth move together
- Focus: short-run vs long-run relationship
- Use time series models to analyze and forecast

VAR = Vector Autoregression (captures short-run dynamics)

VECM = Vector Error Correction Model (captures long-run relationship)
:::

## Data

```{r}
# Fig
ggplot(df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "",
    x = "",
    y = ""
  ) +
  theme_bw()+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 14, face = "bold"),
        legend.position = "none",
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 16))
```

:::{.notes}
- The plot shows the trends in the unemployment rate and GDP growth rate in the United Kingdom over the period from 1985 to 2025.
- The unemployment rate exhibits several peaks and troughs, with notable increases during periods of economic downturn, such as the early 1990s and the late 2000s.
- The GDP growth rate also shows significant fluctuations, with periods of strong growth followed by periods of contraction, particularly during the global financial crisis of 2008-2009.
- The visual comparison of the two series suggests a potential inverse relationship, where increases in the unemployment rate may correspond to decreases in GDP growth, and vice versa. This relationship will be further explored using time series analysis techniques in the subsequent sections of the presentation.
:::

The economic growth rate from 1985 to 2019 shows a more stable pattern, with periods of expansion and mild contractions. The early 1990s recession is evident, as well as the impact of the 2008 financial crisis, which caused a significant dip in growth. Overall, the data indicates that while the UK economy has experienced fluctuations, it has generally maintained positive growth over this period, while unemployment has trended downward with cyclical spikes during economic downturns.
:::

## ADF-test

```{r}
adf_unemployment <- adf.test(unemployment_ts)
adf_gdp <- adf.test(gdp_ts)

# Test for differenced series if the original series is non-stationary
adf_unemployment_diff <- adf.test(diff(unemployment_ts))
adf_unemployment
adf_gdp
adf_unemployment_diff
```

:::{.notes}
Test for stationarity

Results:

- Unemployment: non-stationary
- GDP growth: stationary

A stationary series has stable mean and variance over time.

- I difference unemployment once → becomes stationary

So:

- Unemployment is I(1)
- GDP growth is I(0)

Integrated means the number of differences needed to achieve stationarity. Unemployment is integrated of order 1 (I(1)) because it becomes stationary after differencing once, while GDP growth is already stationary and thus is integrated of order 0 (I(0)). This has implications for the choice of models and the interpretation of relationships between the two series, particularly in terms of cointegration and forecasting.
:::


## ARIMA

```{r}
arima_model <- auto.arima(unemployment_ts)
forecast_arima <- forecast(arima_model, h = 8)
plot(forecast_arima, main = "", xlab = "", ylab = "Unemployment Rate (%)")
```

:::{.notes}
- ARIMA = model using past values

- Used for forecasting unemployment

ARIMA predicts future values using past patterns and trends.

The ARIMA model selected for the unemployment rate is ARIMA(1,1,1), which indicates that the series is differenced once to achieve stationarity, and includes one autoregressive term and one moving average term.

Forecast shows mild increase with uncertainty.

:::

## ARIMA with lagged GDP growth

```{r}
# Create a lagged variable for GDP growth
gdp_lag <- stats::lag(gdp_ts, k = -1)
# Fit a regression model with lagged GDP growth
arimax_model <- auto.arima(unemployment_ts, xreg = gdp_lag)
forecast_arimax <- forecast(arimax_model, xreg = tail(gdp_lag, 8), h = 8)
plot(forecast_arimax, main = "", xlab = "", ylab = "Unemployment Rate (%)")
```

:::{.notes}
ARIMAX = ARIMA + external variable (GDP growth)

The ARIMAX model incorporates lagged GDP growth as an external regressor, allowing us to capture the influence of economic growth on unemployment forecasts. 

- ARIMAX adds economic growth to improve predictions of unemployment.

GDP growth affects unemployment with a lag

- Forecast improves slighlty.
:::

## Accuracy Comparison


```{r}
# Calculate forecast accuracy metrics
accuracy(arima_model)
accuracy(arimax_model)
```

:::{.notes}
ARIMAX performs better:

Lower RMSE
Lower MAE

RMSE = Root Mean Squared Error (measures average magnitude of errors)
MAE = Mean Absolute Error (measures average absolute errors)

Including GDP growth improves forecasting accuracy.
:::

## Cointegration

```{r}
# Use Engle-Granger two-step method
eg_model <- dynlm(unemployment_ts ~ gdp_ts)
e <- resid(eg_model)  # residuals

# Test stationarity of residuals (should be I(0) if cointegrated)
summary(dynlm(d(e) ~ 0 + L(e,1) + L(d(e),1:2)))
```

:::{.notes}
Tests long-run relationship
- Result: No cointegration

Cointegration means two variables move together in the long run.

We find no such relationship.

If cointegration existed, we would use a VECM (Vector Error Correction Model), which combines short-run dynamics with long-run equilibrium.

Since variables are different orders (I(1) vs I(0)), cointegration unlikely

So we move to short-run analysis

:::

## VAR (short run)

```{r}
data_var <- cbind(unemployment_ts, gdp_ts)

lag_selection <- VARselect(data_var, lag.max = 8, type = "const")
#lag_selection$selection

# Fit Var model with selected lag
var_model <- VAR(data_var, p = lag_selection$selection["AIC(n)"], type = "const")
summary(var_model)
```

:::{.notes}
VAR = Vector Autoregression (captures short-run dynamics)

VAR = system of equations where each variable is a function of its own lags and the lags of the other variable.

Each variable depends on its own past values and the past values of the other variable.

Unemployment depends on:

- Past unemployment
- Past GDP growth

GDP growth → negative effect on unemployment

Matches Okun’s Law: higher growth → lower unemployment

:::


## Conclusion

- Unemployment = non-stationary, GDP = stationary

- No long-run relationship (no cointegration)

- Short-run relationship exists

- GDP growth improves unemployment forecasts

- Policy should focus on short-run dynamics

:::{.notes}


:::
